sections.heading: Title
sections.text: DeepJoint is a robust survival model for clinical data. In medicine, the times, ordering, and missingness of observations are not random noise. They reflect how clinicians interact with patients, a phenomenon the authors call clinical presence. When these patterns shift, for example between weekday and weekend admissions, standard prediction models degrade. DeepJoint is a multi-task recurrent network that models three clinical presence processes jointly with the survival outcome, delivering both state-of-the-art discrimination and far greater robustness to changes in the observation process.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: Observational medical data arise from a complex interaction between patients and the healthcare system. When a clinician orders a test, its timing and its very existence carry information about the patient's condition. Most predictive models ignore this, assuming the sampling process is non-informative. This paper argues that ignoring clinical presence leads to sub-optimal, non-transportable models, and that explicitly modelling it is the fix.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: A key challenge of clinical presence is heterogeneity. The same underlying covariate distribution can appear in very different ways depending on the observation process, and that process shifts across countries, over time, and even between weekdays and weekends. The machine learning literature has studied covariate and label shift, but the shift in the observation process itself is under-explored. DeepJoint asks how modelling clinical presence explicitly can make survival models more robust to exactly this kind of shift.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: The paper contributes a deep joint model that treats clinical presence as a multi-task learning problem. A shared recurrent embedding feeds four heads: a longitudinal head, an inter-observation timing head, a missingness head, and a survival head. All are trained together by maximising a combined likelihood with a dynamic weighting scheme. The result is a model whose representation encodes the observation process, giving it both a predictive edge and, more importantly, robustness when that process changes.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: At the core is a Long Short Term Memory network that extracts an embedding from the sequence of laboratory tests observed after ICU admission. This embedding drives three clinical-presence heads. The longitudinal head predicts the next test values under a Gaussian likelihood. The missingness head predicts which tests appear next under a Bernoulli likelihood. The timing head models the inter-observation intensity, giving an exact temporal likelihood. Finally a DeepSurv head models survival under the Cox proportional hazards assumption. The four losses are combined by a dynamic weighting average, controlled by a balance hyperparameter alpha, and optimised end-to-end by gradient descent.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: Experiments use the MIMIC-three intensive-care database, which gathers anonymised laboratory tests, vital signs, and diagnoses for over thirty-eight thousand patients admitted to the Beth Israel Deaconess medical centre between 2001 and 2012. After restricting to patients who survived at least the first twenty-four hours of admission, the cohort contains 30,834 patients. Models predict in-hospital survival from the embedding at the last observation within that first day, and are compared using the time-dependent concordance index and Brier score at one, seven, and fourteen day horizons.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: On a random population split, the three proposed methods deliver competitive-to-best discrimination against models using the same inputs. Strikingly, DeepJoint, which sees only the laboratory values, already outperforms both an LSTM that ignores clinical presence and GRU-D, which explicitly consumes missingness as input. This shows that simply modelling the observation process, even without feeding it in, yields a more predictive embedding. A full fine-tuning step adds a further edge, reaching a C-index of 0.878 at the one-day horizon.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: The paper decomposes its approach into three variants and contrasts them with six baselines. DeepJointFeature, which adds clinical-presence features to the joint model, improves over plain DeepJoint and matches a strong feature baseline. The fine-tuned variant achieves the highest population-level discrimination but is more prone to overfitting when the observation process shifts. Across the robustness experiment, DeepJointFeature is the model that best combines strong discrimination with proximity to the diagonal, meaning its performance transfers most reliably across settings.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: The headline numbers: a time-dependent concordance index of 0.878 at the one-day horizon, evaluated on a cohort of 30,834 MIMIC-three patients. The model jointly captures three dimensions of clinical presence, the longitudinal, timing, and missingness processes, alongside the survival outcome, across prediction horizons of one, seven, and fourteen days.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The one-sentence takeaway: the way clinical data are sampled is itself informative, and jointly modelling that observation process with the survival outcome produces predictions that are not only more accurate but markedly more robust when clinical practice changes. Clinical presence is signal, not noise, and building it into the model is what makes medical predictions transportable.
